p: In the Mishnah (at the beginning of Rosh Hashanah):
"On the first of Nissan is the new year
for kings and for the festivals."
"The festival that falls in it is the new year for the festivals."
This is difficult, for it should have said
"In Nissan is the new year for the festivals."
that for this reason it is called Rosh Chodesh, "the head of the month,"
and not "the beginning of the month":
because it is the head of the entire month.
That is, the entire holiness of the month
And one must sense the holiness
of the festival that falls in it
the head of the entire year.
And this is "the new year for the festivals":
that the holiness of all the festivals
is included in the festival of Pesach.
And this is what is said (Shemos 12:2):
that included in it is the holiness
of all the festivals in all the months.
And this is why the Pesikta opened
with the verse "He made the moon for appointed times"
that is, all the festivals come
through the sanctification of the moon
and are included in the holiness of the month;
for through Hashem Yisbarach having given
to bring holiness into the month,
no holiness is found in it —
only the head of the beis din
they are able to fix all the festivals.
And this is why, before the section of Pesach, it placed first
the mitzvah of sanctifying the month.
And this is what they said
that it was difficult for Moshe,
עַד שֶׁהֶרְאָה לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
until HaKadosh Baruch Hu showed him
We must understand: why did he not learn
the laws of sanctifying the month
after all, all the Sages of Yisrael
and the rules, and why did
Hashem, blessed be His Name, need to show it to him with a finger?
אַךְ נִתְקַשָּׁה מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
But Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him, found it difficult:
when in the Torah no holiness is found in it?
And likewise, how could Yisrael make
עַד שֶׁהֵאִיר לוֹ ה׳ יִתְבָּרַךְ זֶה.
Until Hashem Yisbarach illuminated this for him.
And one may say that for this reason
Rather, the entire essence of the section's concern
And this is "On the first of Nissan
is the new year for the festivals":
the head of all the festivals,
and the body follows the head.
And it says in the Pesikta (there, siman 21):
"He wrapped Himself in a tallis with tzitzis,
and stood Moshe on one side
like the messengers of the month, etc.
He said to them: "In this order, etc.,
and through a tallis with tzitzis."
is what they said in the Mishnah
"The head of the beis din says: Sanctified!"
וְלָמָּה לֹא אָמַר אַב בֵּית דִּין
Why did it not say "av beis din,"
as is the usual usage of the Shas?
that is, that he can attain
and the head is the aspect of
the skull on which the tefillin rest,
that he can attain up to Atika,
which is the attribute of the elder, as is known;
And one who has not left his equal
and can attain up to Atika.
וְכֵן מַה שֶּׁאָמַר עַל יְדֵי עֵדִים
that He showed him, Michael and Gavriel;
for the words of the angels
and so too the witnesses must aim at
the truth that is desired for this,
in the will of Atika Kadisha.
And this is what they said in the Pesikta (there, siman 2):
Your wonders and Your thoughts toward us, etc."
and intercalate the leap years, etc.,
and then He handed them over to them.
and so it is expounded in the Yerushalmi
(רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה פֶּרֶק א הֲלָכָה ג ז:)
the aspect of the supernal Wonder
from Atika, which is covered and hidden.
And this is what they said (Rosh Hashanah 25a):
And this is the secret of what they said (there, 20a):
even though they did not see it,
and they coach them to say what is untrue;
Rather, the head of the beis din,
that it must be so for that time,
and this is the supernal will.
And this is what He showed him:
עַל יְדֵי זָקֵן וְעַל יְדֵי עֵדִים
through an elder and through witnesses,
and the whole matter is from the wonders.
And upon wrapping oneself in it we say
You have clothed Yourself in majesty and splendor,
wrapping Yourself in light like a garment, etc."
that the King is in ten garments,
which He emanated for the creation of the world.
the first garment as "majesty and splendor,"
that is, "Who wraps Himself in light like a garment."
This corresponds to "Let there be light,"
which corresponds to the attribute of Chochmah,
that HaKadosh Baruch Hu wrapped Himself in it
And "majesty and splendor" is the first garment,
(this was explained at the beginning of Parshas Chayei Sarah
And this is the encompassing light
that one merits through a tallis with tzitzis,
And through the tallis with tzitzis
the head of the beis din merits
the shining forth of the aspect of Atika,
and to bring holiness into the month;
holiness is brought into the festivals,
from the light of Atika, as mentioned above.
And this is what Moshe Rabbeinu found difficult,
עַד שֶׁהֶרְאָה לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא.
until HaKadosh Baruch Hu showed him.
And this is "This month shall be for you
that this is the preparation for Pesach,
so that they can make a holy convocation.
And from Rosh Chodesh one must
that will come in this month;
and this is the new year for the festivals,
all the holiness of the festivals.
When Rosh Chodesh falls on a weekday,
one must read on the Shabbos
for on the Shabbos before it
that will be in the weekdays after it,
as we have said many times,
that Shabbos includes all the holinesses
that will come in the weekdays after it,
"He blessed it above all the days," etc.
is the holiness of Rosh Chodesh,
which includes the festival in it,
which is the root of all the festivals.
And when Rosh Chodesh falls on Shabbos,
we read the section on that Shabbos,
and then the holiness is doubled:
for the holiness of Shabbos receives
from the holiness of Rosh Chodesh,
as we said on what they said
because it is sanctified by Yisrael;
And they said in the Gemara (there):
is effective for its own musaf offerings,
but for the Shabbos musaf offerings is not?"
receive the holiness from one another.
the holiness of the festival that comes after it
will be greater than in any other year,
through the reading of the section

paragraphs.text: Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 1:1 — “There are four new years. On the first of Nisan is the new year for kings and for the pilgrimage festivals. On the first of Elul is the new year for the tithe of animals; Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon say: On the first of Tishrei. On the first of Tishrei is the new year for years, for sabbatical years and jubilee years, for planting and for vegetables.” The Mishnah groups together distinct annual beginnings. Rav Tzadok asks why the first of Nisan is called the beginning of the festival cycle when Pesach itself begins later in the month.

paragraphs.text: Rosh Hashanah 4a — “‘For the pilgrimage festivals’—are the festivals on the first of Nisan? They are on the fifteenth of Nisan! Rav Chisda said: The festival that falls in it is the new year for the pilgrimage festivals. Its practical consequence concerns one who vows, so that he becomes subject to ‘You shall not delay’; this follows Rabbi Shimon.” The following teaching requires the three festivals in their order, beginning with Pesach, for Rabbi Shimon’s rule concerning delayed fulfillment of a vow. Rav Tzadok develops the calendar’s head as containing the sanctity of the subsequent cycle.

paragraphs.text: Pesikta Rabbati 15 — “‘He made the moon for appointed times; the sun knows its setting.’ Rabbi Yochanan said: Only the orb of the sun was created to give light, for ‘lights’ is written defectively. If so, why was the moon created? To sanctify through it the beginnings of months and years.” The opening of the HaChodesh Pesikta assigns the moon a calendrical function. Rav Tzadok reads that function as the capacity to impart sanctity to the festivals through the sanctification of the month.

paragraphs.text: Menachot 29a — “The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught: Three things were difficult for Moshe until the Holy One, blessed be He, showed them to him with His finger: the menorah, the new moon, and creeping creatures. The menorah, as it is written, ‘This is the work of the menorah’; the new moon, as it is written, ‘This month shall be for you, the beginning of months’; creeping creatures, as it is written, ‘This shall be unclean for you.’” The teaching links the demonstrative “this” to the divine showing. Rav Tzadok’s question is what difficulty remained beyond the astronomical and legal rules of seeing the new moon.

paragraphs.text: Shemot Rabbah 15:28 — “‘This month shall be for you’—this is one of four things that the Holy One, blessed be He, showed Moshe with His finger, because he found them difficult. He showed him the making of the anointing oil ... He showed him the making of the menorah ... He showed him the creeping creatures ... and the moon, as it is said, ‘This month shall be for you.’” This Midrash includes the anointing oil in its enumeration, whereas Menachos 29a lists three things in the basic teaching. Both attach the moon to a divine demonstration.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Emor 3 — “Even so, the holiness of the festivals depends on Yisrael, who bring holiness into those days by fixing Rosh Chodesh, and this is beyond comprehension: that they can bring holiness into time.” This names exactly what Moshe found hard. It was not the reckoning. It was that human beings can make time holy, a thing beyond understanding.

paragraphs.text: Pesikta Rabbati 15 — “The Holy One, blessed be He, wrapped Himself in a garment with tzitzis. He placed Moshe on this side and Aharon on that side, called Michael and Gavriel, and made them like emissaries of the month. He said to them: ‘On which side did you see the moon—before the sun or after the sun, to its north or to its south? How high was it, where did it incline, and how wide was it?’ He said: ‘In this order that you have seen, so shall My children intercalate the year below: through an elder, through witnesses, and through a garment with tzitzis.’” The checked digital text says “intercalate the year,” while the manuscript paraphrases the procedure as sanctifying the month. The three elements—elder, witnesses, and garment—are expressly present. Rav Tzadok interprets their spiritual significance; the Pesikta’s traditional internal §21 is the manuscript’s locator.

paragraphs.text: Berakhot 63a — “He said to them: ‘Did not Akiva ben Yosef intercalate years and establish months outside the Land?’ They replied: ‘Leave Rabbi Akiva aside, for he left no one like him in the Land of Israel.’ He said: ‘I too left no one like me in the Land of Israel.’ They replied: ‘The kids you left have become horned he-goats, and they sent us to you.’” Chanina, the nephew of Rabbi Yehoshua, had been establishing the calendar abroad. The reply distinguishes Rabbi Akiva’s exceptional position from Chanina’s present claim. Rav Tzadok explains the exceptional leader as the head of all Israel.

paragraphs.text: Pesikta Rabbati 15 — “Rabbi Simon said: ‘Your reckonings are toward us.’ During all those two thousand four hundred and forty-eight years, before Israel went out of Egypt, the Holy One, blessed be He, sat and calculated reckonings, intercalated intercalations, sanctified years, and renewed months. Once Israel went out of Egypt, He handed these over to them, as it is said: ‘Hashem spoke to Moshe and to Aharon ... This month shall be for you.’ What is ‘saying’? He told them: ‘From now on, the beginnings of the months are entrusted to you.’” The Midrash reads the Psalm’s machshevosecha, “Your thoughts,” through calendrical reckoning. Rav Tzadok links the preceding “Your wonders” to the concealed divine root from which that authority proceeds.

paragraphs.text: Rosh Hashanah 25a — “‘You’—even if unwitting; ‘you’—even if deliberate; ‘you’—even if misled. With these words he said to him: ‘Akiva, you have comforted me; you have comforted me.’” Rabbi Akiva expounds the repeated word atem in the festival verses to uphold the court’s calendar. The episode concerns Rabbi Yehoshua’s submission to Rabban Gamliel’s determination despite his own calculation.

paragraphs.text: Rosh Hashanah 20a — “Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: They put pressure on witnesses concerning a moon seen at its expected time in order to make the month full, but do not put pressure on witnesses concerning a moon not seen at its expected time in order to sanctify it. Is that so? Rabbi Yehudah Nesi’ah sent Rabbi Ami: ‘Know that throughout Rabbi Yochanan’s life he taught us: They put pressure on witnesses concerning a moon not seen at its expected time in order to sanctify it; although they did not see it, they say, ‘We saw it.’’ Abaye said: There is no difficulty: one case concerns Nisan and Tishrei, and the other concerns the remaining months.” The sugya gives distinctions and variant reports; Rav Dimi of Nehardea subsequently transmits the rule in the reverse form. Rav Tzadok invokes the striking formulation in his explanation of the court’s access to the divine will, rather than erasing the surrounding discussion’s qualifications.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Emor 3 — on “you, even if unwitting, even if deliberate, even if misled”: “the unwitting and misled are surely called mikra, by chance, yet they bring holiness into these times, and the deliberate as well.” This develops Rav Tzadok’s point. The beis din’s declaration works even against the facts, because it draws on a will above reckoning.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Arizal, Sha'ar HaKavanos, Derushei HaTzitzis 2 — “The tallis itself, from which the tzitzis come out and on which they hang, is the aspect of the encompassing light (or makif) over all of Z'eir Anpin.” This is the Kabbalistic source for Rav Tzadok’s statement. The tallis carries a light above the inner attributes, which fits its role in drawing down Atika to sanctify the month.

paragraphs.text: Bereshit Rabbah 3:4 — “Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak asked Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman: ‘Since I have heard that you are a master of aggadah, from where was light created?’ He replied: ‘It teaches that the Holy One, blessed be He, wrapped Himself in it like a garment, and the radiance of His splendor shone from one end of the world to the other.’ He said this in a whisper. The other said: ‘It is a complete verse: ‘He wraps Himself in light like a garment,’ and you tell it to me in a whisper?’ He replied: ‘As I heard it in a whisper, so I have told it to you in a whisper.’” The garment of light expresses a divine manifestation that shines outward. Rav Tzadok distinguishes it from the prior garment of majesty and splendor.

paragraphs.text: Pri Tzaddik, Chayei Sara 1:3 — “The Holy One emanated ten attributes for the creation of the world. This is what is counted in the Midrash ... and in the Pesikta, ‘I will greatly rejoice,’ according to the Yalkut’s reading: ten garments that the Holy One wore from the day He created the world. These are the ten sefiros, ten garments. The Pesikta counts majesty and splendor as the first garment. This corresponds to the supreme crown, by which they are connected at the root. Afterward it says, ‘He wraps Himself in light like a garment’—the utterance ‘Let there be light,’ which corresponds to wisdom.” This is the internal cross-reference named in the manuscript. Chanukah 2:4 develops the same distinction between the concealed first utterance and the light through which wisdom first becomes accessible.

paragraphs.text: Siddur Ashkenaz, Shabbos Maariv, middle blessing — “You sanctified the seventh day to Your name, the culmination of the making of heaven and earth. You blessed it above all days and sanctified it above all seasons. So it is written in Your Torah.” The prayer describes Shabbos as blessed above all other days and sanctified above all other seasons. Rav Tzadok uses it when explaining how Shabbos encompasses the holiness that will unfold during the following weekdays.

paragraphs.text: Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah 25:1 — “From the Holy One’s side, the sanctity of Shabbos is certainly higher than the sanctity of the month; therefore it says, ‘On the Shabbos day it shall open, and on the day of the month it shall open,’ for there it speaks of what the Holy One will open. ... But from Israel’s side, the sanctity of the month is dear to them because Israel sanctifies it, and a person prefers his own measure.” This explicitly cited maamar explains why the month can be called more sanctified in the sacrificial comparison even though Shabbos has its fixed sanctity from God. It supplies the distinction between divine gift and Israel’s sanctifying work.

paragraphs.text: Zevachim 91a — “Come and hear: The additional offerings of Shabbos precede the additional offerings of Rosh Chodesh. Does Rosh Chodesh confer benefit on its own additional offerings, but confer no benefit on the additional offerings of Shabbos?” The sugya weighs the claims of greater frequency and greater sanctity. Its reply refuses to restrict the day’s added sanctity to one set of offerings: the Shabbos offerings are offered on Rosh Chodesh too. Rav Tzadok reads this shared effect as a mutual reception of sanctity.
